title: Love that lets go
hookLine: sometimes love means letting someone go

lines: THE CAR PACKED TO THE ROOF.
cards: The car is packed to the roof. A lamp, a laundry basket, a box marked kitchen in thick marker. A parent stands in a dorm hallway that smells of fresh paint, and the hardest part of the day is not the stairs.
It's walking back to the car alone. Every instinct says stay one more hour, fix one more shelf. And the kid, very kindly, is already looking past them at the people down the hall.
Nothing has gone wrong. This is what it looks like when everything went right.

teach.h: HE DIVIDED UNTO THEM HIS LIVING.
teach.b: Start with a story Jesus tells in the Gospel of Luke, known as the prodigal son. Look at the beginning, not the well-known ending.

The younger son asks for his share of the family money early, while his father is still alive. In the King James Bible: "Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living."
No lecture is recorded. No conditions. The father lets him go.
When the son finally turns back, the story says the father saw him while he was "yet a great way off." Some readers notice what that suggests: he had been watching the road.
In that reading, letting go didn't mean he stopped loving; he loved without holding the door shut. Third, a different shelf of the Bible.

teach.h: A TIME TO REFRAIN FROM EMBRACING.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes sets life out as a list of seasons, and two of its lines land right here: "a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing," and "a time to keep, and a time to cast away."
The book doesn't say which time you're in, only that both are real.
Fourth, Buddhist teaching has a word for the opposite of this kind of love: clinging.
In the Buddha's first sermon, craving is named as the origin of suffering, and love that clings starts to squeeze. Letting go isn't coldness. It's love that has stopped needing to own.
The father, the seasons, the open hand: releasing someone can be an act of love, not the end of it.

how: People on many paths practice letting go in their own ways: Christians may entrust someone to God in prayer, Buddhist teachers speak of loosening clinging in meditation, and families mark leavings with blessings, meals or small rituals.

o: a story about a son punished for wasting money
the parable of a father who lets his son go, then welcomes him
a parable warning parents never to let children leave

games.q: who let go, and how — tap the pairs.
p: a time to refrain from embracing
craving as the origin of suffering
the father sees his son coming home

s: in Luke's story, the father refuses to hand over the share
the text says simply: he divided unto them his living.
Ecclesiastes lists a time to embrace and a time to refrain
both lines sit side by side in its list of seasons.
in Buddhist teaching, letting go means not caring
the teaching is about loosening clinging, not about stopping love.

games.q: you're the father. your younger son asks for his share of everything, now, while you're still alive. what do you do?
o: refuse, and tell him he isn't ready.
divide the living and let him go.
give it, but follow him to keep watch.
games.why: he divides his living, and the son leaves. no lecture is recorded. later the father sees him "yet a great way off". some readers take it that he had kept watching the road.

practice: Let your hands rest wherever they fall, and bring to mind one person you're holding tightly right now: a child growing up, a friend moving away, someone whose choices aren't yours to make, someone who has already gone.

If your hands have curled, let them rest open on your knees, and hold that person in mind with the grip eased a little, still caring. If you pray, you can place them in God's keeping in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Prodigal son. The parable where a father lets his son go, then watches the road, loving without holding the door shut. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a time, a season, the word Ecclesiastes uses in its list of seasons.

carryVoice: Your line: let go, lovingly. An open hand can still be a loving one. See you tomorrow.
